prompt:
# Write one behaviour-tree node that ADJUSTS an existing navigator

You are writing a single node for the behaviour tree of a Unitree Go2 quadruped
navigating an indoor space it has no map of.

Below the node is an inherited, pretrained, **frozen** locomotion policy. The
only thing anything ever sends the robot is a Twist — `(vx, vy, wz)`. You never
touch the policy, the gait, or the joints.

**You are not writing the navigator.** A navigator already exists, it already
drives, and it will keep driving whether or not your node does anything. Your
node sits above it and revises what it asked for.

Return **one Python module**, in one fenced ```python block, and nothing else
that looks like code. Everything you want to say in prose, say outside the
fence. What the module must contain is set out in "What to return" at the end.

## How the tree runs: a layered command pipeline

Every node in the tree ticks, **every step, in order**. Nothing short-circuits
anything.

    Layer[ ports, BASE, node_1, node_2, ... ]
             ^      ^      ^
             |      |      `- each may revise the fields it declared
             |      `-------- proposes a whole command, every tick
             `--------------- publishes a few facts from the sensors

The **base** is a general indoor navigator. It gets the robot most of the way
most of the time, it handles the awkward cases, and it never declines to act.
Each later node may then adjust individual fields of what the base proposed.

This is subsumption: a competent low layer, refined by narrow higher ones. Your
node is one of the higher ones.

**So the thing you are writing is small.** It does one thing to one part of the
command, under one condition, and the rest of the time it stays out of the way.

## The one hard rule: you declare which fields you may write

Your class declares `WRITES` — the Twist fields it is allowed to touch:

```python
WRITES = ("vx",)            # may bound or set forward speed, nothing else
WRITES = ("wz",)            # may steer, but may not change speed
WRITES = ("vx", "wz")       # both. Only if the mechanism genuinely needs both.
```

This is **enforced, not advisory.** Writing a field you did not declare raises
immediately and the node is rejected. Declare the smallest set your mechanism
actually needs — a node that declares all three is claiming to be a navigator,
and it will be judged as one.

Two ways to write, and they are the only two:

```python
ports.cap(vx=0.35)       # min(|pending|, 0.35), sign kept. Never speeds up.
ports.adjust(wz=0.8)     # replaces the field outright. Last writer wins.
```

Prefer `cap` whenever the mechanism is a limit, a bound, or a "no faster than"
— it composes with other caps in any order, which `adjust` does not.

And you can see what the base asked for:

```python
pending = ports.command          # a Command(vx, vy, wz). Never None when you
                                 # tick, because the base ticks before you.
if pending.vx > my_limit:
    ports.cap(vx=my_limit)
```

**Do not call `ports.drive(...)`.** That writes the whole command and is the
base's job; it raises for a node that narrowed `WRITES`.

## Declining is a first-class outcome, and it is free

Return `Status.FAILURE` from `precondition`, or simply write nothing in `tick`,
and the base's command passes through **byte-identical**. The robot behaves
exactly as if your node were not in the tree.

That matters more than it sounds. Your node's contribution is measured by adding
it to the tree and re-running the same worlds: it can only be credited for the
episodes it changes, and it is blamed for every episode it breaks. A node that
acts only when its trigger genuinely holds is a good node. A node that fires on
every tick has replaced the base rather than supported it, and it will be
measured as having done so.

## The node contract

A leaf is one of three kinds, and the kind is the class you subclass:

- **`Condition`** — answers one question about the world and publishes it as a
  port. Never touches the Twist.
- **`Action`** — the only kind that may touch the Twist. With a narrowed
  `WRITES` it is a *modifier*, which is what you are writing.
- **`Decorator`** — wraps exactly one child and governs whether the child runs.
  Never touches the Twist itself.

Your class declares, as class attributes:

| Attribute | What it is |
|---|---|
| `WRITES` | the Twist fields this node may write. See above. |
| `PORTS` | a tuple of `Port` — the typed interface between nodes. See below. |
| `PRECONDITION` | one sentence: when this node applies |
| `EFFECT` | one sentence: what this node changes |
| `TAGS` | a tuple of short strings, for retrieval |

and implements:

```python
def reset(self, scenario, rng):    # clear per-episode state. optional.
def precondition(self, obs, ports) -> bool:   # default: always True
def tick(self, obs, ports) -> Status:         # Status.SUCCESS / FAILURE / RUNNING
```

**One precondition and one effect.** A node that needs two of either is two
nodes. This is not a style rule: contribution is measured by adding one node at
a time, and a node with two effects is attributable to neither.

**No coupling to a specific scenario.** Your node will be run on procedurally
generated worlds you have never seen. It may not name a room, a coordinate, a
doorway or a map. Anything it knows about the world it learns through `obs` at
tick time.

### Ports

Ports are how nodes pass information to each other. They are **not** a
blackboard: at tick time you are handed a `PortView` restricted to exactly the
ports you declared, and touching anything else raises immediately.

```python
Port(name, PortType.X, Direction.IN)    # you read it:   value = ports["name"]
Port(name, PortType.X, Direction.OUT)   # you write it:  ports["name"] = value
```

The port vocabulary is **closed**. These seven types and no others:

| `PortType` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `POSE` | `(x, y, yaw)` — a belief about where the robot is, never ground truth |
| `BEARING` | radians, robot frame unless the port name says otherwise |
| `SPEED` | m/s, non-negative |
| `RANGES` | an array of beam returns, metres |
| `CONFIDENCE` | `[0, 1]` — how much to trust something |
| `FLAG` | a boolean fact about the episode |
| `REGION` | an area of the floor, `(x, y, radius)` |

Three ports are always published before your node ticks, so you may declare any
of them as inputs: `goal_known` (FLAG), `pose` (POSE), `ranges` (RANGES).
Anything else you declare as an input must be published by another node earlier
in the Layer, and if nothing does, the tree refuses to build.

Publish an OUT port when the quantity you computed is genuinely useful to
someone else — a limit, a bearing, a confidence. Do not publish your own
internal state.

### What to import

Exactly these, and nothing else.

```python
import math
import numpy as np

from core.observation import Command
from nodes.contract import (Action, Condition, Decorator, Direction, Port,
                            PortType, Status)
```

Import only what you use. You will usually not need `Command` at all: a modifier
revises fields, it does not construct commands.

### What your node can see

`tick` is handed an `Observation`, frozen, one per control step:

```python
obs.t                   # sim seconds since the episode started
obs.ranges              # np.ndarray, 181 beams, metres, inf where no return
obs.range_angles        # np.ndarray, beam bearings in the ROBOT frame, radians
obs.range_max           # 6.0 — what "as far as I can see" means
obs.pose_estimate       # (x, y, yaw) — the BELIEF about our pose, not the truth
obs.pose_error_estimate # scalar, metres — how wrong we think the belief is
obs.contact             # bool — are we touching something right now
obs.goal                # (x, y), or None meaning NOT DISCLOSED
```

Two of these are traps and both are deliberate:

- **`pose_estimate` is a belief.** On some scenarios a seeded random walk is
  added to it and it drifts away from the truth. Ground truth is never in
  `Observation`; the runner keeps it for scoring only.
- **`obs.goal` may be `None`**, meaning the goal exists and the episode is still
  scored against it, but this robot has not found it yet. It **latches**: once
  disclosed it stays disclosed. Your node runs on scenarios that withhold the
  goal and on scenarios that do not, so **handle `None` explicitly**. Do not
  assume a tuple.

The scan is 181 beams over a full circle, so `obs.ranges[0]` is not the front —
find the beam you want through `obs.range_angles`.

Speeds are saturated by the runner to `|vx|, |vy| <= 0.8 m/s` and
`|wz| <= 1.0 rad/s`. Asking for more is not an error; it is just clipped.

## The task family this node has to be useful for

Reach a goal whose position is known, in an indoor space with no map. Walls and furniture occlude; the route is not a straight line and the obstruction is often not visible until the robot is close to it.

## What to base the node on

A principle card has been written for this task. **Implement this principle and
nothing else.**

```yaml
id: shape_anchored_goal_address
node_name: ReanchorGoalToVisibleShape

mechanism: A place is specified as an address on a metric frame built from the arrangement of surfaces as surfaces - the shape of the environment - and that address is couched in displacement properties: the metric distances and angles from the target to those surfaces, plus sense (which surface is to the left and which to the right). Cheng shows this frame outranks the two obvious alternatives. It outranks featural identity: in Experiment 3 a diagonal transposition, which scrambles the distances, angles and handedness of the feature arrangement but leaves the target's relations to the surfaces intact, produced no decrement in any rat, whereas an affine transformation or a reflection, which leaves the local feature on the target but moves the target to a geometrically different corner, produced a significant decrement in every rat (p < .05, .01, .001). And it outranks dead reckoning: rats kept a vestibular record of how far the box had been rotated during the delay, yet "the retention and use of both featural and inertial information are subsidiary to the use of the geometric relations between the target and the shape of the environment" (p. 161) - when the two disagreed the rats went to the geometrically correct place. This helps because the surface arrangement is re-measured directly at recall time, so an address expressed in it does not accumulate the error that an address expressed in an integrated-motion frame does. Its one failure mode is the price of the same property: when the shape admits two congruences with itself, the address names two places, and the animal takes the wrong one about as often as the right one (47% correct vs 31% rotational, Table 1).

trigger: The goal position is disclosed, the belief about our own pose is no longer trustworthy, and enough surface is currently visible to define a metric frame whose sense is decidable. Concretely: goal is not None, pose_error_estimate exceeds the trust threshold, a shape frame was latched earlier while the belief was still trustworthy, and the currently visible surface arrangement is still recognisably the one that was latched. If any of these fails - goal undisclosed, belief still good, too few returns, shape near-symmetric so sense is undecidable, or the visible arrangement has changed - the leaf returns FAILURE and the tree falls through to steering by pose_estimate.

derivation: Mapping. Cheng's "arrangement of surfaces as surfaces" becomes the set of finite lidar returns: 181 beams, anything with r < range_max is a surface point, inf is no surface. His "inertial/vestibular record" becomes pose_estimate, which is the drifting integrated-motion belief, with pose_error_estimate as the robot's own confession of how far it has drifted. His "featural information" (brightness, texture, odour of a panel) has no counterpart on a planar lidar and is dropped - this card claims nothing about features. The paper's target-to-shape address becomes the goal's coordinates in a frame computed from the scan. All of this mapping is mine; Cheng never discusses range sensors, partial visibility or a moving observer.
Building the frame (each control step). Take the finite returns and convert to robot-frame points p_i = (r_i*cos(theta_i), r_i*sin(theta_i)) using range_angles. Require N >= 40 of the 181 beams finite, else abstain - fewer than that is not an arrangement of surfaces, it is a corridor mouth. Centroid c = mean(p_i). Second-moment matrix M = sum (p_i - c)(p_i - c)^T / N, with eigenvalues lam1 >= lam2 and unit eigenvectors. Let e1 be the major eigenvector and set e2 = rot90(e1) so the pair is always right-handed; that right-handedness is how sense is carried, which Cheng (p. 171) says the rat carries too, and which is why the frame must never be built by an operation that is blind to reflection.
Resolving the rotational ambiguity. e1 is defined only up to sign, and the two signs are exactly Cheng's target and its rotational equivalent. Break the tie with a statistic that a 180-degree-symmetric shape cannot supply: the third moment along the axis, m3 = sum ((p_i - c).e1)^3 / N. Choose the sign of e1 that makes m3 >= 0. If the normalised skew |m3| / lam1^1.5 < 0.05, the visible shape is too close to 180-degree symmetric for sense to be decided, and the leaf abstains rather than committing. The rat commits and is wrong 31 times in 100 (Table 1, p. 158); a robot that abstains keeps the drifting belief, which is bad, instead of a confidently mirrored address, which is worse. The 40-beam minimum and the 0.05 skew threshold are mine; the paper states no threshold of either kind.
Latching the address. While pose_error_estimate <= 0.30 m the belief is treated as trustworthy. On any such step, express the goal offset in the shape frame: d = R(-yaw) * (goal - (x,y)) from pose_estimate, then u = (d - c).e1, v = (d - c).e2. Store (u, v) together with a shape signature (lam1, lam2, N). The 0.30 m trust threshold is mine, chosen as roughly half the Go2's body length, on the reasoning that a belief wrong by less than half a body is not yet what is making the robot miss.
Using the address. Once pose_error_estimate > 0.30 m, recompute c, e1, e2 and the signature from the live scan. Accept the frame only if |lam1/lam1_latched - 1| <= 0.25 and |lam2/lam2_latched - 1| <= 0.25 - the same arrangement of surfaces, seen from somewhere else, not a different room. Then reconstruct the goal in the robot frame as g = c + u*e1 + v*e2 and steer to that instead of to the pose-derived offset. Twist: psi = atan2(g_y, g_x), wz = clip(2.0*psi, -1.0, 1.0), vx = 0.8*cos(psi) if |psi| <= 1.0 rad else 0.0, vy = 0.0. The 0.25 signature tolerance and the steering gains are mine. When the signature test fails, the leaf abstains and re-latches at the next step where pose_error_estimate <= 0.30 m.
Where the mapping breaks, plainly. Cheng's box is fully visible from every point inside it, so his metric frame is global and permanent. A 6 m lidar in an indoor space sees one room's worth of surface, so this frame is local and temporary: it corrects drift accumulated since the latch, while the same surfaces stay in view, and it cannot correct drift accumulated before the latch or survive a doorway. That limitation is a property of the sensor, not of the paper, and it is the main reason this card's confidence is not high.

prediction:
  statement: On runs where pose_estimate drifts, steering the final approach by the goal's address in the shape frame rather than by the pose belief raises the fraction of episodes that reach the goal, because the address is re-measured against visible surfaces every step instead of inheriting accumulated belief error.
  metric: goal_reached
  baseline: goal_seeker
  min_effect: 0.1
  cost_metric: path_length
```

The fields mean what they say, and each one has a job:

- **mechanism** — what happens, and why it helps. This is the node body.
- **trigger** — when it applies. This is the precondition, and under the layered
  pipeline it is doing real work: outside the trigger your node must leave the
  base's command alone.
- **derivation** — how the principle becomes a rule for a Go2 with a 181-beam 2D
  scan. Where the derivation and your instincts disagree, follow the derivation:
  it is what the card is for.
- **prediction** — the falsifiable claim. **Restate it verbatim** in
  `PREDICTION`: the metric, the baseline and the minimum effect are the card's,
  not yours.
- **node_name** — what the leaf is called. Use it as the class name.

You are not told where this principle came from, and you do not need to know.
A card is a card: extracted from a paper, recalled from one, or devised from
nothing, it is implemented the same way and judged by the same harness.

If you believe a different mechanism would score better, that belief is not what
is being measured here — a node that quietly implements something else makes the
card untestable.

**If the principle genuinely cannot be expressed as an adjustment to an existing
navigator, say so in prose and write the closest honest version you can.** Some
mechanisms are whole navigators and this pipeline cannot represent them; that is
a finding about the corpus, and it is more useful than a node that pretends.

Two steps, both automatic, neither of which you can talk round.

1. **Validity.** Your module is loaded, wired into

2. **Contribution.** The tree above is run over a suite of randomly generated

You do not write the worlds and you have never seen them. There is no
micro-world to build and no baseline to name — that is deliberate, because a
generator that writes both the mechanism and the world that judges it is

## Rules the candidate is checked against

Your module is rejected, automatically, if any of these is false. The rejection

- It parses, and it imports **only** from this list:

- It defines **exactly one** `Condition`, `Action` or `Decorator` subclass.
- Every port type is one of the seven. `EFFECT` and `PRECONDITION` are non-empty.
- `WRITES` names only `vx`, `vy` and `wz`, and the node writes nothing outside

I couldn't write or run anything (the sandbox denied file writes and shell approval in this non-interactive session), so the module below is checked by eye rather than by `py_compile`. Notes on the choices that aren't forced by the card:

- **`WRITES = ("vx", "wz")`.** The mechanism is a *substitution of the steering target*, so `wz` genuinely has to be replaced (`adjust` — the whole claim is that the shape-frame bearing beats the belief-derived one). `vx` is only ever *bounded*: I used `cap(vx=0.8*cos psi)` rather than a set, because at `psi≈0` the card's value is exactly the runner's saturation ceiling, so a cap reproduces the card's "turn in place beyond 1.0 rad, crawl while swinging on" behaviour while never overriding a base that has slowed for an obstacle. `vy` is left to the base; the card's `vy = 0.0` would mean claiming a third field to write a value the base almost certainly already holds.
- **The precondition is only the disclosure clause.** The latch has to run on precisely the steps where the node *doesn't* act (belief still trustworthy), so gating the whole tick on "belief has drifted" would mean there is never an address to use. The remaining trigger clauses — beam count, skew/sense decidability, latch present, signature match — are checked inside `tick`, and every one of them returns `FAILURE` having written nothing.
- **One OUT port.** `shape_anchored_goal_bearing` is published only on the steps where the node acts, since that is the only time the quantity exists; the latched `(u, v)` and the signature are internal state and are not published.
- **Honest limit:** this corrects drift accumulated *since* the latch, while the same surfaces stay in view. It cannot survive a doorway, and it will abstain (not mirror) in corridors and near-symmetric rooms. `path_length` is the real cost — re-anchoring can swing the heading off the base's route and it turns in place above 1.0 rad of heading error.

```python
"""Shape-anchored goal address (Cheng): re-measure the goal against visible surfaces."""

import math

import numpy as np

from nodes.contract import Action, Direction, Port, PortType, Status


class ReanchorGoalToVisibleShape(Action):
    """Steer the final approach by the goal's address in a locally measured shape frame.

    Mechanism (Cheng's geometric module): while the pose belief is still
    trustworthy, the goal is written down not as map coordinates but as an
    address on a metric frame built from the arrangement of visible surfaces --
    the centroid and principal axes of the finite lidar returns, with sense
    fixed by the third moment along the major axis so the frame is not blind to
    reflection.  Once the belief has drifted, that address is re-measured
    against the surfaces visible *now*, so it does not inherit the error the
    integrated-motion belief has accumulated since the latch.

    Revises `wz` (adjust: the heading to the re-anchored goal replaces the
    heading the base derived from the drifted belief -- that substitution is the
    point of the node) and bounds `vx` (cap: no faster than 0.8*cos(psi), i.e.
    crawl or stop while swinging onto the corrected bearing).  `vy` is left
    entirely to the base.

    Declines -- writing nothing, so the base's command passes through
    byte-identical -- when the goal is undisclosed, when the belief is still
    good (<= 0.30 m error; those steps are used to latch the address instead),
    when fewer than 40 beams return a surface, when the visible shape is too
    near 180-degree symmetric for its sense to be decided, when no address was
    ever latched, or when the surfaces in view no longer match the latched
    signature (we have left the room the address was written in).
    """

    WRITES = ("vx", "wz")

    PORTS = (
        Port("goal_known", PortType.FLAG, Direction.IN),
        Port("ranges", PortType.RANGES, Direction.IN),
        # The corrected goal bearing is useful to anything else that wants to
        # know where the goal is without going through the drifting belief.
        Port("shape_anchored_goal_bearing", PortType.BEARING, Direction.OUT),
    )

    PRECONDITION = (
        "The goal position has been disclosed, so a goal address can either be "
        "latched onto the visible surface arrangement or read back off it."
    )
    EFFECT = (
        "While the pose belief is untrustworthy, replaces the commanded heading "
        "with the bearing to the goal reconstructed from the latched shape-frame "
        "address, bounding forward speed by the cosine of the heading error."
    )
    TAGS = ("geometry", "shape-frame", "drift", "relocalisation", "goal-approach")

    # --- thresholds (all from the card's derivation) ----------------------
    MIN_SURFACE_BEAMS = 40      # fewer than this is a corridor mouth, not an arrangement
    TRUST_RADIUS_M = 0.30       # a belief wrong by less than half a body is not the problem
    MIN_NORMALISED_SKEW = 0.05  # below this the shape is too symmetric to give sense
    SIGNATURE_TOL = 0.25        # same surfaces seen from elsewhere, not a different room
    HEADING_GAIN = 2.0
    MAX_WZ = 1.0
    CRUISE_VX = 0.8
    MAX_HEADING_FOR_FORWARD = 1.0  # rad; beyond this, turn in place

    def reset(self, scenario, rng):
        self._address = None    # (u, v) of the goal in the latched shape frame
        self._signature = None  # (lam1, lam2, n_beams) of the latched arrangement

    def precondition(self, obs, ports):
        # Only the disclosure clause lives here: the remaining trigger clauses
        # are checked inside tick, because the *latch* has to run on exactly the
        # steps where the node does not act.
        return bool(ports["goal_known"]) and obs.goal is not None

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
    # shape frame
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
    def _shape_frame(self, obs):
        """Centroid and right-handed, sense-resolved axes of the visible surfaces.

        Returns (c, e1, e2, lam1, lam2, n) in the robot frame, or None if the
        scan does not define a frame whose sense is decidable.
        """
        r = np.asarray(obs.ranges, dtype=float)
        ang = np.asarray(obs.range_angles, dtype=float)
        hit = np.isfinite(r) & (r > 0.0) & (r < float(obs.range_max))
        n = int(np.count_nonzero(hit))
        if n < self.MIN_SURFACE_BEAMS:
            return None

        rr = r[hit]
        aa = ang[hit]
        pts = np.stack((rr * np.cos(aa), rr * np.sin(aa)), axis=1)

        c = pts.mean(axis=0)
        q = pts - c
        m = (q.T @ q) / n
        vals, vecs = np.linalg.eigh(m)  # ascending eigenvalues, orthonormal vectors
        lam2, lam1 = float(vals[0]), float(vals[1])
        if lam1 <= 1e-9:
            return None
        e1 = np.asarray(vecs[:, 1], dtype=float)

        # e1 is defined only up to sign, and the two signs are exactly the
        # target and its rotational equivalent. Break the tie with a statistic
        # that a 180-degree-symmetric shape cannot supply.
        proj = q @ e1
        m3 = float(np.mean(proj ** 3))
        if m3 < 0.0:
            e1 = -e1
            m3 = -m3
        if m3 / (lam1 ** 1.5) < self.MIN_NORMALISED_SKEW:
            return None  # abstain rather than commit to a possibly mirrored address

        e2 = np.array((-e1[1], e1[0]), dtype=float)  # rot90: the pair carries sense
        return c, e1, e2, lam1, lam2, n

    def _goal_offset_from_belief(self, obs):
        """Goal in the robot frame according to the (drifting) pose belief."""
        gx, gy = float(obs.goal[0]), float(obs.goal[1])
        px, py, yaw = (float(v) for v in obs.pose_estimate)
        dx, dy = gx - px, gy - py
        cs, sn = math.cos(-yaw), math.sin(-yaw)
        return np.array((cs * dx - sn * dy, sn * dx + cs * dy), dtype=float)

    def _signature_matches(self, lam1, lam2):
        lam1_l, lam2_l, _ = self._signature
        if lam1_l <= 1e-9 or lam2_l <= 1e-9:
            return False
        return (abs(lam1 / lam1_l - 1.0) <= self.SIGNATURE_TOL
                and abs(lam2 / lam2_l - 1.0) <= self.SIGNATURE_TOL)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
    def tick(self, obs, ports):
        frame = self._shape_frame(obs)
        if frame is None:
            return Status.FAILURE
        c, e1, e2, lam1, lam2, n = frame

        if float(obs.pose_error_estimate) <= self.TRUST_RADIUS_M:
            # Belief still good: write the address down (overwriting any older
            # one) and let the base drive. This branch never touches the Twist.
            rel = self._goal_offset_from_belief(obs) - c
            self._address = (float(rel @ e1), float(rel @ e2))
            self._signature = (lam1, lam2, n)
            return Status.FAILURE

        if self._address is None or not self._signature_matches(lam1, lam2):
            # Never latched, or these are not the surfaces the address was
            # written against. Fall through to steering by pose_estimate; a
            # later trustworthy step will re-latch.
            return Status.FAILURE

        u, v = self._address
        g = c + u * e1 + v * e2
        psi = math.atan2(float(g[1]), float(g[0]))

        ports["shape_anchored_goal_bearing"] = psi

        wz = max(-self.MAX_WZ, min(self.MAX_WZ, self.HEADING_GAIN * psi))
        ports.adjust(wz=wz)

        # A bound, not a set: the base may already be going slower (obstacle,
        # doorway) and this node has no business speeding it up.
        if abs(psi) <= self.MAX_HEADING_FOR_FORWARD:
            ports.cap(vx=self.CRUISE_VX * math.cos(psi))
        else:
            ports.cap(vx=0.0)

        return Status.SUCCESS

    "statement": (
        "On runs where pose_estimate drifts, steering the final approach by the "
        "goal's address in the shape frame rather than by the pose belief raises "
        "the fraction of episodes that reach the goal, because the address is "
        "re-measured against visible surfaces every step instead of inheriting "
        "accumulated belief error."
    ),
    "metric": "goal_reached",
    "baseline": "goal_seeker",
    "min_effect": 0.1,
    "cost_metric": "path_length",
}
```

One caveat worth recording against the card rather than the code: the principle is stated as a *localisation* claim ("the address is re-measured every step"), but this pipeline can only express it as a steering override, so the node is credited or blamed for heading choices rather than for the pose correction itself. The reconstruction `g = c + u·e1 + v·e2` is used directly as a steer target with no obstacle term — that is the card's Twist, and it is why `path_length` is the honest cost: on a route where the base was correctly arcing around furniture, an abrupt re-anchor can point the robot back at the wall it was skirting, and only the base's later ticks (or the following episode's caps) recover it.
